study.title: Acts 1 - The beginning of the church after the ascension of Jesus
study.overview: Acts 1 opens the second account of Luke concerning Jesus and the community that was born of his work. The chapter bridges the gap between Jesus" earthly life and the apostolic mission: recalls the resurrection with evidence, the instruction on the Kingdom of God, the promise of the Holy Spirit, the ascension, the obedient waiting in prayer and the replacement of Judas by Matthias. The focus is not on chronological curiosity, but in preparing the disciples to witness with power and to show that the expansion of the gospel begins under the direction of the exalted Christ himself and the fulfilled Scriptures.

outline.title: Prologue and the hope of the Holy Spirit
outline.explanation: Luke recalls that his first book dealt with what Jesus began to do and teach until ascension. Jesus appears alive after suffering, proves his resurrection in many ways, and forty days speaks about the Kingdom of God. Before leaving, he orders the disciples to wait in Jerusalem for the Father's promise: they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit, not just with water.

outline.title: The question about the Kingdom and the ascension
outline.explanation: The disciples ask whether Jesus would restore the kingdom to Israel at that time, but he redirects their attention: it is not up to them to know times and occasions determined by the Father. Instead, they would receive power from the Holy Spirit to be witnesses of Jesus of Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Then Jesus is raised in their eyes, and two men in white robes announce that he will return in the same way as he has been seen to come up.

outline.title: The community gathered in prayer
outline.explanation: The disciples return from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and gather in the upper room. The text lists the remaining eleven apostles and shows a persevering, unanimous group in prayer and supplication, together with the women, Mary, the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. The church appears here as a people still small, but united and praying, awaiting the action of God.

outline.title: The Fall of Judas and the Choice of Matthias
outline.explanation: Peter interprets Judas' betrayal in the light of the Scriptures and states that it was necessary to fulfill what the Holy Spirit had foretold by David. Judas had participated in the ministry, but lost his position; the camp attached to his guilt became known as the Blood Field. Then Peter establishes the criterion for choosing a substitute: someone who had accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to ascension and could witness the resurrection. After prayer, they cast lots, and Matthias is counted with the eleven apostles.

study.context: The chapter is presented as a continuation of Luke's gospel, addressed to Theophilus. The notes highlight that Theophilus was probably a high social position and possibly a patron. The immediate setting is Jerusalem and its surroundings, especially the Mount of Olives, and the training community brings together about one hundred and twenty people. The text also shows historical transition: from Jesus" earthly ministry to the apostolic witness and to the coming of the Holy Spirit.
study.theology: Acts 1 teaches that the resurrection of Jesus is central and publicly confirmed, not a peripheral detail. The Kingdom of God remains the axis of the message of Jesus, but the disciples do not receive control over the times of God; they receive a mission. The Father's promise is fulfilled in the Holy Spirit, which is the source of power for Christian witness. The ascension affirms the exaltation of Jesus and his future coming, which prevents merely nostalgic or speculative faith: the church lives between the departure and the return of the Lord. We also see the authority of the Scriptures in Peter's reading of Judas, and the humble dependence of God on prayer before the decision on Matthias. The chapter also suggests that the community of Jesus must be marked by unity, perseverance and witness, not by isolated human impulse.

scholarViews.insight: The key verse of the chapter shows the geographical expansion of the good news: from Jerusalem and Judea to Samaria and the ends of the earth, and the Holy Spirit is the source of power for this mission.

The disciples' question reveals the expectation of restoration of the kingdom, but Jesus' answer corrects them and calls them to observe obedience to God's plan, rather than speculating on times and seasons.
The release of luck is understood as an ancient and simple method to decide the choice, made after prayer, and Matthias is counted among the eleven apostles.

questions: Why does Jesus answer the question about the kingdom not with a date, but with a promise of power and mission?
What does unity in prayer, before Pentecost, teach you about how the church should act when you are awaiting God's direction?
How does Matias' choice show dependence on God and commitment to the testimony of the resurrection?
study.practice: This chapter calls the church to exchange unproductive curiosity for practical fidelity. Today, this means seeking the filling of the Holy Spirit to witness to Christ with courage, to remain in prayer with other brothers, to value communion and to submit important decisions to God's direction. He also reminds us of living with hope in the return of Jesus, without trying to control the divine calendar. A concrete application is to separate regular time for community prayer and for the intentional witness of Christ in our immediate context, beginning where God has already placed us.
study.uncertainty: The text and the notes provided only allow us to state that Theophilus was probably a high social position and possibly patron of Luke; it is not possible to safely identify who he was. The notes also do not solve all the details about the exact mode of the release of luck, they only describe it as an old procedure used in prayer. There is not enough basis, in the notes provided, to broaden the historical context beyond what the chapter explicitly presents.
